directAnswer: St. Eusebius was bishop of Rome for only a few months around 309–310, in the uneasy years just before Constantine came to power. His short reign was consumed by a bitter dispute over how to readmit Christians who had lapsed during the Diocletianic persecution, and the emperor Maxentius exiled him to Sicily, where he died. The Church honors him as a saint on August 17.

paras: Eusebius inherited a Roman church still bruised by the Great Persecution. Many believers had denied the faith or handed over sacred books under pressure, and once the danger eased they asked to return. Eusebius held to the position of his predecessor Marcellus: the lapsed could be reconciled, but only after doing real penance.

A rival party led by a man named Heraclius demanded easier terms, and the conflict grew loud enough to disturb public order in the city. Our clearest witness is not a chronicle but a verse epitaph that Pope Damasus later composed for his tomb, which speaks of sedition, strife, and the exile of both leaders.

sections.h2: Exile Under Maxentius and Burial in the Catacomb of Callixtus
paras: To end the unrest, Maxentius banished Eusebius and Heraclius alike. Eusebius was sent to Sicily and died there after a brief time, which is why later tradition counted him among those who suffered for the faith even though he was not executed.

His remains were afterward returned to Rome and laid in the Catacomb of Callixtus on the Appian Way. Beyond these points, details are thin. The Liber Pontificalis describes him as a Greek and the son of a physician, but that book was compiled long after his death, and the exact length and dates of his reign remain uncertain.

keyFacts: Reigned only a few months, c. 309–310
Defended penance as the condition for readmitting the lapsed
Exiled to Sicily by the emperor Maxentius and died there
Buried in the Catacomb of Callixtus; honored in an epitaph by Pope Damasus
Feast day: August 17

faqs.question: Why was Pope Eusebius exiled?
faqs.answer: Roman Christians were deeply divided over how to treat believers who had lapsed during persecution. Eusebius insisted on penance, a rival named Heraclius opposed him, and the resulting disorder led Emperor Maxentius to banish both men.

faqs.question: How do we know about Pope Eusebius?
faqs.answer: The main source is a verse inscription written decades later by Pope Damasus for his tomb, along with brief entries in early papal lists and the Liber Pontificalis. Little else survives.

directAnswer: St. Miltiades, also spelled Melchiades, was pope from 311 to 314 and the first bishop of Rome to see the Church move from persecution to toleration under Constantine. In 313 he presided over a synod at the Lateran that judged the Donatist dispute in North Africa in favor of Bishop Caecilian of Carthage. Ancient sources describe him as African by birth, and his feast is kept on January 10.

sections.h2: From Persecution to the Edict of Milan
paras: Miltiades was elected in 311, after a vacancy that followed the exile of Eusebius. The situation of Roman Christians was already shifting: Maxentius, who controlled Rome, allowed property confiscated from the Church to be returned, and Miltiades sent deacons to recover it from the city prefect.

In October 312, Constantine defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge. The following year, Constantine and his co-emperor Licinius issued the arrangement known as the Edict of Milan, granting Christians freedom of worship and the restoration of their churches. Miltiades thus became the first pope to lead the Roman church in the open, without fear of the state.

sections.h2: The Lateran Synod of 313 and the Donatists
paras: In North Africa, a party later called the Donatists refused to accept Caecilian as bishop of Carthage, claiming that one of his consecrators had betrayed the faith during persecution. They appealed to Constantine, who referred the matter to the bishop of Rome.

Miltiades convened bishops from Italy and Gaul in the autumn of 313. They met in a residence of the empress Fausta on the Lateran, property that soon passed to the Church and became the site of the papal cathedral. The synod upheld Caecilian and condemned Donatus. Miltiades reportedly sought a conciliatory settlement, offering to recognize bishops from the opposing side where only one claimant existed.

The Donatists did not accept the verdict, and the dispute continued at the Council of Arles in 314 and for generations afterward. Later Donatist polemic even accused Miltiades himself of having been a traitor during persecution, a charge St. Augustine took pains to refute.

The Liber Pontificalis calls Miltiades an African and attributes to him a rule against fasting on Sundays and Thursdays, along with other disciplinary decrees; historians treat such attributions cautiously, since the work was compiled centuries later.

He died in January 314 and was buried in the Catacomb of Callixtus. Though early lists sometimes counted him as a martyr, he died in peace at the very moment the age of the martyrs was closing, which gives his short reign its particular place in Church history.

keyFacts: Pope from 311 to 314; described as African by birth
First pope to serve after Constantine's victory and the Edict of Milan (313)
Presided over the Lateran synod of 313, which ruled against the Donatists
The synod met in the Lateran residence later given to the Church
Buried in the Catacomb of Callixtus; feast day January 10

faqs.question: Why is Pope Miltiades also called Melchiades?
faqs.answer: Both spellings appear in ancient manuscripts. Miltiades is the form generally preferred by historians, while Melchiades appears in many older Latin texts and calendars.

faqs.question: What did the Lateran synod under Miltiades decide?
faqs.answer: Meeting in 313 at the Lateran, the bishops under Miltiades confirmed Caecilian as the rightful bishop of Carthage and condemned the claims of Donatus, though the Donatist division in Africa continued long afterward.

faqs.question: Was Pope Miltiades a martyr?
faqs.answer: No. Some early lists honored him with martyr language, but he died peacefully in 314, after Constantine had ended the persecution of Christians.

directAnswer: St. Sylvester I was pope from 314 to 335, the long reign that coincided with Constantine's patronage of the Church. Under him the first great Roman basilicas were built, including St. John Lateran and the original St. Peter's, and the Council of Nicaea met in 325 with his legates present. Later legends made him the baptizer of Constantine and the recipient of the forged Donation of Constantine; neither claim is historical.

sections.h2: Bishop of Rome in Constantine's Empire
paras: Sylvester, a Roman, succeeded Miltiades in January 314 and led the Roman church for almost twenty-two years. That was the period when Christianity moved from a tolerated minority to a faith enjoying imperial favor, and Rome's Christian landscape changed dramatically.

Surprisingly, few of his own writings or decisions survive. The emperor, not the pope, dominated the great ecclesiastical events of the day, and Sylvester appears in the record mostly through his representatives and the churches built during his time.

sections.h2: Arles, Nicaea, and the Papal Legates
paras: Months into his reign, a council at Arles in Gaul met to reconsider the Donatist controversy. Sylvester did not attend but sent two priests and two deacons, and the bishops sent him a letter reporting their decisions.

In 325, Constantine convened the first ecumenical council at Nicaea in Asia Minor to answer the teaching of Arius, who denied that the Son is fully divine. Sylvester, elderly and far away, was represented by two Roman priests, Vitus and Vincentius. The council produced the Nicene Creed, professing the Son to be of one substance with the Father, and settled the method for dating Easter.

Imperial generosity transformed Rome during these years. The Lateran Basilica, today the cathedral of the bishop of Rome, rose beside the former Lateran palace. Over the tomb of St. Peter on the Vatican Hill, construction began on the great basilica that stood until it was replaced in the sixteenth century. A church inside an imperial residence, later known as Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, was associated with relics of the Cross.
The Liber Pontificalis also credits Sylvester with founding a parish church on land given by a priest named Equitius, a foundation connected with the later church of San Martino ai Monti.

sections.h2: Legends: The Baptism of Constantine and the Donation
paras: A fifth-century tale, the Acts of Sylvester, claims that he cured Constantine of leprosy and baptized him in Rome. In fact, Constantine was baptized near the end of his life in 337, near Nicomedia, by Bishop Eusebius of Nicomedia.

That legend fed the Donation of Constantine, a document most likely forged in the eighth century, in which the emperor supposedly granted Sylvester and his successors authority over Rome and the western provinces. It was cited for centuries in disputes over papal power until fifteenth-century scholars, notably Lorenzo Valla, demonstrated that it could not be authentic.

Sylvester died on December 31, 335, and was buried in the Catacomb of Priscilla. His feast falls on the last day of the year, which is why New Year's Eve is called Silvester in much of Europe; Eastern Christians honor him on January 2.

keyFacts: Pope from 314 to 335, during the reign of Constantine
Sent legates to the Council of Arles (314) and the Council of Nicaea (325)
His reign saw the building of the Lateran Basilica and Old St. Peter's
The Donation of Constantine attributed to him is a medieval forgery
Feast day December 31 in the West, January 2 in the East

faqs.question: Did Pope Sylvester I baptize Constantine?
faqs.answer: No. That story comes from a later legend. Historical sources show Constantine was baptized shortly before his death in 337 by Eusebius of Nicomedia.

faqs.question: Did Pope Sylvester attend the Council of Nicaea?
faqs.answer: He did not travel to Nicaea. He was represented by two Roman priests, Vitus and Vincentius, who took part in the council on his behalf.

faqs.question: Why is New Year's Eve called Silvester in some countries?
faqs.answer: Sylvester died on December 31, 335, and his feast is celebrated that day. In Germany, Austria, Poland, and elsewhere, the last night of the year is still named after him.

directAnswer: St. Mark was a Roman who served as pope for less than a year, from January to October 336, near the end of Constantine's reign. The Liber Pontificalis credits him with founding the church of San Marco in Rome and a basilica at the Catacomb of Balbina, where he was buried. His feast day is October 7.

sections.h2: Two Churches Linked to Pope Mark
paras: Mark's pontificate lasted only about eight months, and the surviving record is brief. According to the Liber Pontificalis, he built two churches: one inside the city, the ancestor of today's Basilica of San Marco near Piazza Venezia, and a cemetery basilica on the Via Ardeatina at the Catacomb of Balbina.

Archaeologists have since identified the remains of a funerary basilica in that area that is thought to be his. The same source lists gifts of land and liturgical vessels that Constantine reportedly made to these foundations, typical of the generous patronage of the period.

sections.h2: The Bishop of Ostia and the Roman Calendars
paras: The Liber Pontificalis also says Mark decreed that the bishop of Ostia should consecrate each new pope and granted him the pallium. Ostia's bishop did hold that role in later centuries, but historians doubt that the custom began with Mark himself.

Some scholars connect his time with the earliest Roman lists of the burial dates of bishops and martyrs, preserved in a calendar compiled in 354. That link is a reasonable hypothesis rather than a documented fact. Mark died on October 7, 336, and was buried in the basilica he had founded. Little more about his life is known.

keyFacts: Pope from January to October 336
Credited with founding the Roman church of San Marco
Built a cemetery basilica at the Catacomb of Balbina, where he was buried
Tradition links him to the bishop of Ostia's role in consecrating popes
Feast day: October 7

faqs.question: Is the Basilica of San Marco in Rome named after Pope Mark?
faqs.answer: It is dedicated to St. Mark the Evangelist, but tradition holds that Pope Mark founded the original church there in 336, and his relics were later kept in it.

faqs.question: Was Pope Mark a martyr?
faqs.answer: No. He served after the persecutions ended and died a natural death in October 336. He is honored as a saint, not as a martyr.

directAnswer: St. Julius I was pope from 337 to 352 and one of the firmest Western defenders of the Nicene faith during the Arian crisis. He received the exiled St. Athanasius of Alexandria in Rome, declared him innocent at a Roman synod, and wrote a famous letter to Eastern bishops about the role of the Roman see in such disputes. Tradition also credits him with founding Santa Maria in Trastevere.

paras: Julius was elected in February 337, a few months before Constantine's death. Although the Council of Nicaea had condemned Arianism in 325, sympathizers of Arius remained powerful in the East, and they targeted the leading champions of the Nicene creed.

Chief among those champions was Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, whom opposing bishops had deposed and driven out. Around 339 he came to Rome, joining other exiled bishops, including Marcellus of Ancyra, who sought a hearing there.

sections.h2: The Roman Synod and Julius's Letter to the East
paras: Julius invited the Eastern bishops to Rome to make their case. They declined, and around 341 a Roman synod examined the charges and found Athanasius and Marcellus innocent, restoring them to communion.

Julius then wrote to the bishops gathered at Antioch, a letter preserved because Athanasius copied it into his own defense. In it Julius rebuked them for acting without consulting Rome and stated that, by custom, matters touching the church of Alexandria should be brought to the bishop of Rome so that a just decision might proceed from there. Historians regard the letter as an important early witness to Rome's appellate role.

To resolve the standoff, the emperors Constans and Constantius II summoned a council at Serdica, today Sofia, around 343. Julius sent legates rather than attending in person. The Eastern bishops withdrew and held their own assembly, while the Western bishops again cleared Athanasius.

Serdica also issued canons allowing a deposed bishop to appeal to the bishop of Rome, who could order a new hearing. Those canons were later cited, sometimes under the mistaken label of Nicene canons, in disputes between Rome and other churches. In 346 Athanasius was finally able to return to Alexandria, and Julius sent a warm letter to the Alexandrian church on his homecoming.

The Liber Pontificalis attributes several churches to Julius, among them a basilica near the Forum and one across the Tiber. The latter is traditionally identified with Santa Maria in Trastevere, one of the oldest churches in Rome dedicated to the Virgin Mary.

Julius died on April 12, 352, and was buried in the Catacomb of Calepodius on the Via Aurelia. The list of Roman bishops' burials compiled in 354 includes his name, one of the early documents that help historians date the popes of this century.

keyFacts: Pope from 337 to 352
Received and vindicated St. Athanasius at a Roman synod (c. 341)
His letter to the bishops at Antioch is an early witness to Roman primacy
Represented by legates at the Council of Serdica (c. 343)
Traditionally credited with founding Santa Maria in Trastevere; feast day April 12

faqs.question: Why did Pope Julius I support St. Athanasius?
faqs.answer: Athanasius was the leading defender of the Nicene Creed against Arianism. After examining the charges against him at a Roman synod, Julius found him innocent and received him into communion despite opposition from Eastern bishops.

faqs.question: What churches did Pope Julius I build?
faqs.answer: According to the Liber Pontificalis, he founded several basilicas. Tradition links him especially to Santa Maria in Trastevere, which ranks among Rome's oldest Marian churches.

faqs.question: Where is Pope Julius I buried?
faqs.answer: He was buried in the Catacomb of Calepodius on the Via Aurelia, west of Rome. His relics were later moved to Santa Maria in Trastevere.

directAnswer: Liberius was pope from 352 to 366, during the struggle between the Nicene faith and the Arian-leaning policies of Emperor Constantius II. He refused at first to condemn St. Athanasius and was exiled to Thrace, but ancient writers report that he later made concessions that allowed him to return to Rome. He is the earliest pope not listed as a saint in the Latin Church, though Eastern Christians honor him on August 27.

paras: When Liberius became pope in 352, Constantius II ruled the whole empire and was determined to secure the condemnation of Athanasius of Alexandria. Councils at Arles in 353 and Milan in 355 bowed to imperial pressure, and even the papal legates at Arles gave way.

Liberius refused to add his name. He insisted that Athanasius could not be condemned without a fair hearing and that the faith of Nicaea must be upheld. In 355 he was seized, brought before the emperor, and sent into exile at Beroea in Thrace. In his absence, the archdeacon Felix was installed in Rome, a figure the Church later counted as an antipope.

Liberius returned to Rome in 358. Writers such as Athanasius, Hilary of Poitiers, and Jerome report that the hardships of exile wore him down and that he accepted the condemnation of Athanasius and signed a creed drafted at Sirmium that avoided the Nicene language. Which formula he signed, and whether letters attributed to him from this period are authentic, remain debated by historians.

The Catholic tradition has noted that whatever Liberius signed under duress was not a free act of teaching addressed to the whole Church. The episode was nonetheless remembered as a painful moment, and it is one reason he was never added to the Roman calendar of saints.

sections.h2: Return to Rome and Reconciliation with Nicaea
paras: Romans welcomed Liberius back enthusiastically, and Felix was soon forced out. After Constantius died in 361, Liberius openly supported the Nicene faith once more. He worked to reconcile bishops who had compromised at the Council of Rimini in 359, provided they now professed the creed of Nicaea.
Near the end of his life, he received a delegation of Eastern bishops who accepted the Nicene Creed and restored them to communion, a sign of how far the tide had turned.

sections.h2: The Liberian Basilica and the Liberian Catalogue
paras: Liberius is credited with a basilica on the Esquiline Hill, known as the Basilica Liberiana. The present Santa Maria Maggiore was built in the following century under Sixtus III, and the story of a miraculous August snowfall marking its site is a medieval legend.

His name also survives in the Liberian Catalogue, a list of popes ending with him that was included in a Roman calendar compiled in 354. It is one of the most valuable early sources for papal chronology. Liberius died on September 24, 366, and the disputed election that followed led to violent conflict between the supporters of Damasus and Ursinus.

keyFacts: Pope from 352 to 366
Exiled to Beroea in Thrace in 355 for refusing to condemn St. Athanasius
Ancient writers report he yielded to imperial pressure before returning in 358
Gave his name to the Liberian Catalogue, an early list of popes
Not on the Latin calendar of saints; honored in the East on August 27

faqs.question: Why is Pope Liberius not a saint in the Catholic Church?
faqs.answer: He is not listed in the Roman Martyrology, largely because of reports that he gave in to Emperor Constantius II during his exile. Eastern Christian churches, however, venerate him as a saint.

faqs.question: Did Pope Liberius teach heresy?
faqs.answer: Ancient sources say he signed an ambiguous creed and condemned Athanasius under duress, but the details are disputed. It was not a free, formal teaching to the Church, and after his return he again supported the Nicene faith.

faqs.question: Is Santa Maria Maggiore the Liberian Basilica?
faqs.answer: Santa Maria Maggiore is often linked to the Basilica Liberiana, but the present church was built under Pope Sixtus III in the fifth century. The snow legend about its founding is a later tradition.

directAnswer: St. Damasus I was pope from 366 to 384, a period when Christianity became the official religion of the Roman Empire. He commissioned St. Jerome to revise the Latin Bible, work that led to the Vulgate, honored the martyrs with verse inscriptions in the catacombs, and strengthened the authority of the Roman see. His reign began with a violent, contested election against the rival claimant Ursinus.

paras: When Liberius died in 366, two factions chose two bishops. One group consecrated the deacon Ursinus, while a larger party elected Damasus, a deacon who had served under Liberius. Fighting broke out between their supporters, and the pagan historian Ammianus Marcellinus records that over a hundred people were killed in a single day at one of the basilicas.

The civil authorities backed Damasus and expelled Ursinus, though his followers troubled Rome for years. The episode cast a shadow over the beginning of the pontificate and was raised against Damasus by his enemies long afterward.

Around 382, the scholar Jerome came to Rome and served as Damasus's secretary. The pope asked him to revise the existing Latin translations of the Gospels, which varied widely in quality. Jerome began with the Gospels and later, after leaving Rome, went on to translate much of the Old Testament from Hebrew.

The result, known as the Vulgate, became the standard Bible of the Latin Church for more than a thousand years. A list of the books of Scripture is traditionally associated with a Roman synod Damasus held in 382, though scholars debate how much of the surviving text dates from his time.

Damasus loved the memory of Rome's martyrs. He restored their tombs in the catacombs, improved access for pilgrims, and composed Latin verse epitaphs in their honor. The calligrapher Furius Dionysius Filocalus carved them in a distinctive and elegant lettering style.

Many of these inscriptions survive in whole or in fragments, including one in the crypt of the popes at the Catacomb of Callixtus. They are among our most important sources for several early popes and martyrs, including his predecessor Eusebius.

sections.h2: Rome's Place in an Imperial Church
paras: In 380, the emperor Theodosius I issued the Edict of Thessalonica, ordering all subjects to follow the faith handed down by St. Peter to the Romans and professed by Damasus and by Bishop Peter of Alexandria. Around the same time, Emperor Gratian stopped using the pagan title Pontifex Maximus, a gesture of distance from the old state religion.

The Council of Constantinople in 381, later counted as the second ecumenical council, met without Western participation. Damasus did not attend, but Roman synods under him condemned Arian and Apollinarian errors, and his doctrinal statements circulated widely. He also emphasized that Rome's primacy rested on the words of Christ to Peter, not on the decisions of councils.

Damasus died on December 11, 384, and was buried in a church he had built on the Via Ardeatina. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a Spaniard, and Portuguese tradition associates his family with the ancient town of Egitania, today Idanha-a-Velha.

keyFacts: Pope from 366 to 384, after a violent contested election with Ursinus
Commissioned St. Jerome to revise the Latin Gospels, the start of the Vulgate
Wrote verse epitaphs for martyrs, carved by Furius Dionysius Filocalus
Named in the Edict of Thessalonica (380) as a standard of orthodox faith
Feast day: December 11

faqs.question: What was Pope Damasus I's role in the Vulgate?
faqs.answer: He asked St. Jerome, his secretary, to revise the Latin Gospels around 382. Jerome's work, later extended to most of the Bible, became the Vulgate, the Latin Church's standard Scripture text for centuries.

faqs.question: What are the Damasian inscriptions?
faqs.answer: They are Latin verse epitaphs Damasus wrote for martyrs and popes buried in Rome's catacombs. Carved in a distinctive script by Filocalus, many still survive and are valuable historical sources.

faqs.question: Was Pope Damasus I from Portugal?
faqs.answer: The Liber Pontificalis describes him as Spanish, and a Portuguese tradition links his family to Egitania in Lusitania. He was probably born in Rome, where his father served as a priest.

directAnswer: St. Siricius was pope from 384 to 399 and the author of the earliest papal decretal that survives complete, a letter to Bishop Himerius of Tarragona in Spain. In that and later letters he gave binding rulings on baptism, penance, ordination, and the continence of clergy. He also condemned the monk Jovinian and dedicated the rebuilt Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls.

sections.h2: The Letter to Himerius of Tarragona
paras: Siricius, a Roman who had served as a deacon under Liberius and Damasus, was elected in December 384. Soon after, a letter from Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, arrived asking about disciplinary questions in the Spanish churches. Siricius answered in a letter usually dated to early 385.

This reply is the oldest surviving papal decretal, an authoritative ruling meant to be observed as law. It addressed whether converts baptized by Arians needed rebaptism (they did not, but were received by the laying on of hands), set Easter and Pentecost as the normal seasons for baptism, regulated public penance, and laid down requirements for those seeking ordination.

The decretal is best known for insisting that bishops, priests, and deacons live in perpetual continence. Many clergy at that time were married, and Siricius did not dissolve those marriages, but he required that married clergy abstain from relations with their wives after ordination.

He presented this not as a novelty but as an obligation flowing from the service of the altar. Historians regard the letter as the first papal decree on the subject, and it shaped Western discipline on clerical celibacy for centuries. A Roman synod in 386 repeated similar rules and communicated them to the bishops of Africa.

Around 390, a monk named Jovinian taught that virginity was no holier than marriage and that fasting brought no special merit. Siricius condemned him at a Roman synod, and St. Ambrose and the bishops of Milan concurred. At the same time, Siricius defended the dignity of marriage against extreme ascetic views.

His relationship with Jerome was cool. Jerome left Rome in 385, not long after Siricius's election, and later wrote of him without warmth. With Ambrose, the dominant bishop of northern Italy, Siricius maintained cooperative ties.
The emperors had begun building a much larger basilica over the tomb of St. Paul on the road to Ostia. In 390 Siricius dedicated it, and an inscription naming him is still preserved in the basilica.
Siricius died on November 26, 399, and was buried in the Catacomb of Priscilla on the Via Salaria. His feast is kept on that day.

keyFacts: Pope from 384 to 399
Wrote the oldest surviving papal decretal, to Himerius of Tarragona (c. 385)
First papal decree requiring continence of bishops, priests, and deacons
Condemned Jovinian at a Roman synod around 390
Dedicated the rebuilt St. Paul Outside the Walls in 390; feast day November 26

faqs.question: What is a papal decretal, and why is Siricius important for it?
faqs.answer: A decretal is a papal letter giving an authoritative ruling on a point of church discipline. Siricius's letter to Himerius of Tarragona is the oldest one that survives complete.

faqs.question: Did Pope Siricius require priests to be celibate?
faqs.answer: He required bishops, priests, and deacons to live in continence. Married clergy kept their marriages but were to abstain from marital relations after ordination. It was the first papal decree on the matter.

faqs.question: Who was Jovinian, whom Siricius condemned?
faqs.answer: Jovinian was a Roman monk who argued that virginity and fasting had no greater merit than marriage and ordinary living. Siricius condemned his teaching at a Roman synod around 390.

directAnswer: St. Anastasius I was a Roman who served as pope for just over two years, from 399 to 401. He is remembered for condemning the writings of Origen, encouraging the African bishops against Donatism, and, according to the Liber Pontificalis, directing priests to stand with heads bowed during the reading of the Gospel. His feast day is December 19.

paras: Anastasius took office during a heated debate over the third-century theologian Origen, whose speculative ideas had alarmed many bishops. Theophilus of Alexandria urged the West to condemn them, and Jerome pressed the same cause from Bethlehem.

Anastasius obliged. In letters to other bishops, he declared Origen's writings unacceptable to Rome. Rufinus of Aquileia, who had translated Origen into Latin, sent the pope a defense of his own orthodoxy; Anastasius replied that he left Rufinus's conscience to God but did not endorse his project. Jerome praised Anastasius warmly, suggesting that God had taken him early so he would not see the coming disasters that befell Rome.

sections.h2: Africa, the Liturgy, and Family Ties
paras: Anastasius wrote to the bishops of Africa encouraging their efforts against the Donatist schism, which was still dividing that church a century after its start. He also maintained friendly ties with Paulinus of Nola, the poet and bishop.

The Liber Pontificalis credits him with the custom that priests stand, heads bowed, while the Gospel is read, a reverent posture still reflected in the liturgy. Jerome describes his successor, Innocent I, as his son; whether this was meant literally is uncertain. Anastasius died in December 401 and was buried in the Catacomb of Pontian. Beyond these points, little is recorded.

keyFacts: Pope from 399 to 401
Condemned the writings of Origen at the urging of Theophilus and Jerome
Encouraged African bishops in their struggle with Donatism
Credited with the custom of standing with bowed heads for the Gospel
Feast day: December 19

faqs.question: Why did Pope Anastasius I condemn Origen?
faqs.answer: Bishops such as Theophilus of Alexandria and scholars such as Jerome considered certain ideas in Origen's writings dangerous. Anastasius agreed and declared those writings unacceptable to the Roman church.

faqs.question: Was Pope Anastasius I the father of Pope Innocent I?
faqs.answer: Jerome calls Innocent his son, and some historians take this literally. Others think it means a spiritual relationship, and the Liber Pontificalis names a different father, so the matter is uncertain.

directAnswer: St. Innocent I was pope from 401 to 417, through the Visigothic sack of Rome in 410. He defended the exiled St. John Chrysostom, condemned the teachings of Pelagius at the request of the African bishops, and wrote influential letters on the canon of Scripture, confirmation, and the anointing of the sick. He was born at Albano near Rome, and his feast is kept on March 12.

paras: Innocent's reign coincided with the collapse of Roman security in Italy. Alaric's Visigoths besieged Rome more than once, and the emperor Honorius stayed safely at Ravenna. During one round of negotiations, Innocent traveled to Ravenna as part of an embassy from the city seeking terms.

He was still away when Alaric's forces entered and sacked Rome in August 410, the first time the city had fallen to a foreign enemy in some eight centuries. The shock reverberated across the Christian world and later moved St. Augustine to write The City of God. Innocent returned to help the city recover.

In the East, John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople, was deposed in 403 and later exiled through the efforts of Theophilus of Alexandria and the imperial court. John appealed to Innocent, who refused to recognize the deposition and demanded a fair hearing by a council of Eastern and Western bishops.

Innocent sent a delegation to Constantinople, but its members were mistreated and sent back. He broke communion with the bishops responsible. John died in exile in 407, and Innocent restored communion only after his name was restored to the church's commemorations.

The British monk Pelagius taught that human beings could live without sin by their own effort, minimizing the need for grace. In 416, councils at Carthage and Milevis in North Africa, with Augustine among the bishops, condemned his views and asked Innocent to confirm their judgment.

In early 417, Innocent replied that Pelagius and his disciple Caelestius were to be excluded from communion until they repented, and praised the Africans for referring the matter to the Apostolic See. Augustine later spoke of the case as settled once Rome's reply arrived, a remark frequently remembered in simplified form.

In 405 Innocent answered Bishop Exuperius of Toulouse with a list of the books of Scripture that matches the canon later affirmed by the Church. In 416 he wrote to Bishop Decentius of Gubbio about liturgical practice, teaching that the anointing with chrism on the forehead after baptism belongs to bishops and citing the Letter of James on the anointing of the sick.
He also supported the bishop of Thessalonica as his representative in eastern Illyricum. Innocent died on March 12, 417, and was buried in the Catacomb of Pontian.

keyFacts: Pope from 401 to 417; born at Albano near Rome
Rome was sacked by Alaric's Visigoths in 410 while he was at Ravenna
Defended St. John Chrysostom and broke communion with his persecutors
Confirmed the African condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius in 417
Wrote on the canon of Scripture (405) and on confirmation and anointing (416)

faqs.question: Where was Pope Innocent I during the sack of Rome?
faqs.answer: He was in Ravenna, where he had gone as part of an embassy to Emperor Honorius seeking a settlement with Alaric. The city fell in August 410 while he was away.

faqs.question: What did Pope Innocent I decide about Pelagius?
faqs.answer: In 417 he confirmed the judgment of African councils that Pelagius and Caelestius had taught error regarding grace, and declared them out of communion until they repented.

faqs.question: What is Innocent I's letter to Decentius about?
faqs.answer: Written in 416 to the bishop of Gubbio, it explains Roman liturgical customs, including the bishop's role in anointing the baptized with chrism and the anointing of the sick based on the Letter of James.

directAnswer: St. Zosimus was pope for less than two years, from 417 to 418, and is described in early sources as Greek. He reopened the case of Pelagius and Caelestius, at first criticizing the African bishops who had condemned them, but in 418 he issued a formal letter condemning Pelagianism. His reign was also marked by disputes with the African church and with bishops in Gaul.

paras: Zosimus succeeded Innocent I in March 417, only days after Innocent had confirmed the condemnation of Pelagius and his disciple Caelestius. Caelestius promptly came to Rome to plead his case in person, and Pelagius sent a statement of faith.

Impressed by their professions of loyalty, Zosimus wrote to the African bishops suggesting they had acted too hastily, and he gave them time to present clearer evidence. The Africans, led by Aurelius of Carthage and supported by Augustine, responded firmly that Innocent's judgment should stand.

In the spring of 418, a large council at Carthage restated the Church's teaching on original sin and grace, and Emperor Honorius ordered the expulsion of the Pelagian leaders from Rome. Zosimus, after further examination, issued a lengthy circular letter known as the Epistola Tractoria, which condemned Pelagius and Caelestius and required bishops to subscribe to it.

Most bishops did so. A group of Italian bishops led by Julian of Eclanum refused and were deposed. Julian went on to become Augustine's most persistent opponent in writing. The Tractoria survives only in fragments, but it marked the decisive papal rejection of Pelagianism.

sections.h2: Apiarius and the Bishops of Gaul
paras: Zosimus also clashed with Africa over Apiarius, a priest of Sicca deposed by his bishop who appealed to Rome. Zosimus supported the appeal, citing canons he believed came from Nicaea. The African bishops could not find them in their copies of the Nicene canons; they were in fact canons of the Council of Serdica. The dispute dragged on into the next two pontificates.

In Gaul, he granted Bishop Patroclus of Arles sweeping metropolitan rights and made him his representative there. This angered neighboring bishops and was largely undone by later popes. Facing opposition even among his own clergy, Zosimus fell ill and died on December 26, 418. He was buried in the basilica of St. Lawrence Outside the Walls.

keyFacts: Pope from March 417 to December 418; described as Greek by birth
Reopened and then confirmed the condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius
Issued the Epistola Tractoria against Pelagianism in 418
Disputed with African bishops over the appeal of the priest Apiarius
Buried at St. Lawrence Outside the Walls; feast day December 27

faqs.question: Did Pope Zosimus support Pelagius?
faqs.answer: Initially he was persuaded by the professions of faith from Pelagius and Caelestius and asked the African bishops to reconsider. After further evidence and a council at Carthage in 418, he condemned them in the Epistola Tractoria.

faqs.question: What was the Apiarius affair?
faqs.answer: Apiarius was an African priest who appealed his deposition to Rome. Zosimus backed the appeal using canons he attributed to Nicaea, which were actually from Serdica, causing a long dispute with the African church.

faqs.question: Who was Julian of Eclanum?
faqs.answer: He was an Italian bishop who refused to sign Zosimus's condemnation of Pelagianism and was deposed. He became St. Augustine's leading opponent in the later Pelagian debates.

directAnswer: St. Boniface I was a Roman priest who served as pope from 418 to 422. His election was contested by the archdeacon Eulalius, and the emperor Honorius settled the dispute in Boniface's favor. As pope, he supported St. Augustine against the Pelagians and defended Rome's authority over the churches of eastern Illyricum.

paras: After Zosimus died, a group of clergy chose the archdeacon Eulalius on December 27, 418. The next day, a larger body of priests elected Boniface, an elderly priest. The city prefect sided with Eulalius and reported to Emperor Honorius, who at first recognized him.

Honorius then called a synod to decide the matter and ordered both men to stay away from Rome while it deliberated. When Eulalius returned to the city in defiance of the order before Easter 419, the emperor withdrew his support and recognized Boniface, who took full possession of the see that April. Honorius afterward ordered that disputed elections should be resolved by a new election rather than imperial choice between rivals.

Boniface continued the Roman opposition to Pelagianism. Augustine dedicated to him a treatise answering two Pelagian letters that had been circulating, and Boniface encouraged the African bishops' efforts. The Apiarius dispute with Africa remained unresolved during his reign.

He curbed the special powers that Zosimus had given to the bishop of Arles, restoring the rights of other metropolitans in Gaul. When Emperor Theodosius II tried to place eastern Illyricum under the church of Constantinople, Boniface protested, and Honorius persuaded his nephew to keep the earlier arrangement.
Boniface died on September 4, 422, and was buried at the cemetery of St. Felicitas on the Via Salaria. Little else about him is recorded.

keyFacts: Pope from December 418 to September 422
Elected in competition with the archdeacon Eulalius, later considered an antipope
Recognized by Emperor Honorius in April 419
St. Augustine dedicated an anti-Pelagian treatise to him
Buried at the cemetery of St. Felicitas on the Via Salaria

faqs.question: Who was Eulalius?
faqs.answer: Eulalius was a Roman archdeacon elected by a rival faction a day before Boniface. The emperor initially recognized him but later rejected him for defying imperial orders, and he is now counted as an antipope.

faqs.question: How was Pope Boniface I connected to St. Augustine?
faqs.answer: Augustine dedicated his treatise Against Two Letters of the Pelagians to Boniface, who supported the African bishops in opposing Pelagian teaching.

directAnswer: St. Celestine I was pope from 422 to 432 and played a central role in the condemnation of Nestorius, whose teaching was rejected at the Council of Ephesus in 431. He commissioned St. Cyril of Alexandria to act on Rome's judgment and sent legates to the council. He also sent Palladius as the first bishop to the Christians of Ireland.

sections.h2: Nestorius and the Title Mother of God
paras: In 428 Nestorius became archbishop of Constantinople and soon objected to calling the Virgin Mary Theotokos, the God-bearer, preferring titles that separated Christ's divinity from his humanity. Cyril of Alexandria opposed him, and both men wrote to Rome.

In August 430, a Roman synod under Celestine examined Nestorius's views and found them contrary to the faith. Celestine ordered Nestorius to recant within ten days or be removed from communion, and he charged Cyril with carrying out the decision.

sections.h2: Legates to the Council of Ephesus
paras: Emperor Theodosius II summoned a general council to Ephesus in 431. Celestine sent two bishops, Arcadius and Projectus, and the priest Philip, instructing them to uphold the Roman judgment. Cyril opened the council before the legates or the Syrian bishops arrived, and the assembly deposed Nestorius.

When the legates arrived, they confirmed the council's action in the name of the Roman see. Philip spoke of Peter living and judging in his successors, words recorded in the council's acts. The council affirmed that Mary is truly Mother of God. Celestine later urged reconciliation with the Syrian bishops who had resisted the decision.

sections.h2: Palladius, Germanus, and the Defense of Augustine
paras: The chronicler Prosper of Aquitaine records that in 431 Celestine sent Palladius as first bishop to the Irish who believed in Christ. A few years earlier, at the urging of Palladius, then a deacon, Celestine had sent Bishop Germanus of Auxerre to Britain to counter Pelagian teaching there. Later tradition also linked Celestine to St. Patrick's mission, but that connection is not supported by early evidence.

Celestine wrote to bishops in Gaul defending the memory of Augustine, who had died in 430, against critics of his teaching on grace. In another letter he told certain Gallic bishops that clergy should be distinguished from laity by their teaching and conduct rather than by their dress.

During his pontificate, a priest from Illyria named Peter built the Basilica of Santa Sabina on the Aventine Hill. Its dedicatory mosaic inscription, still visible, names Celestine as pope at the time. Celestine also restored Santa Maria in Trastevere after the damage done in 410.
He died on July 27, 432, and was buried in the Catacomb of Priscilla. His feast is kept on July 27 in the Roman calendar; Eastern Christians honor him on April 8.

keyFacts: Pope from 422 to 432
Roman synod of 430 condemned Nestorius; Cyril of Alexandria enforced the ruling
Sent legates to the Council of Ephesus (431), which upheld Mary as Theotokos
Sent Palladius as first bishop to the Christians of Ireland in 431
Santa Sabina on the Aventine was built during his reign

faqs.question: Did Pope Celestine I attend the Council of Ephesus?
faqs.answer: No. He sent legates: the bishops Arcadius and Projectus and the priest Philip. They confirmed the council's deposition of Nestorius in Rome's name.

faqs.question: Did Pope Celestine I send St. Patrick to Ireland?
faqs.answer: Early sources say he sent Palladius as first bishop to the Irish Christians in 431. The idea that he also sent Patrick appears only in later tradition.

faqs.question: Why was the Council of Ephesus important for Marian devotion?
faqs.answer: The council rejected Nestorius's objections and affirmed that Mary is Theotokos, Mother of God, because the child she bore is one divine Person, true God and true man.

directAnswer: St. Sixtus III was a Roman priest who served as pope from 432 to 440. He supported the reconciliation of Cyril of Alexandria with John of Antioch after the Council of Ephesus and built the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore, whose mosaics still bear his name. His feast day is March 28.

sections.h2: Santa Maria Maggiore and the Lateran Baptistery
paras: Sixtus is best remembered as a builder. On the Esquiline Hill he erected the great basilica now called Santa Maria Maggiore, one of the four major basilicas of Rome. The mosaics of its triumphal arch, honoring Mary and the infancy of Christ, carry the inscription Xystus episcopus plebi Dei, Bishop Sixtus to the people of God.

The church is widely seen as a celebration of the Council of Ephesus, which had affirmed Mary as Mother of God the year before his election. Sixtus also rebuilt the Lateran baptistery in its octagonal form, with verse inscriptions on the meaning of baptism that are still preserved.

The Council of Ephesus had left Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch at odds. In 433, they agreed on a joint statement of faith, the Formula of Union, and Sixtus welcomed the reconciliation in letters to both.

Earlier in life, as a Roman priest, Sixtus had been thought sympathetic to Pelagius, but he later opposed the movement, and Augustine wrote to him praising his firmness. As pope, he refused to readmit Julian of Eclanum to communion. He also defended Rome's rights over the churches of Illyricum. Sixtus died on August 18, 440, while the deacon Leo, his eventual successor, was away on a mission in Gaul.

keyFacts: Pope from 432 to 440
Built Santa Maria Maggiore; its arch mosaics bear his name
Rebuilt the octagonal Lateran baptistery
Welcomed the 433 reconciliation between Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch
Feast day: March 28

faqs.question: Did Pope Sixtus III build Santa Maria Maggiore?
faqs.answer: Yes. The present basilica was built under Sixtus III, and the mosaic inscription on its triumphal arch names him as the bishop who dedicated it to the people of God.

faqs.question: How was Pope Sixtus III connected to the Council of Ephesus?
faqs.answer: He became pope the year after the council, celebrated its teaching on Mary through Santa Maria Maggiore, and supported the reconciliation of the Alexandrian and Antiochene churches in 433.

directAnswer: St. Leo I, called the Great, was pope from 440 to 461 and is a Doctor of the Church. His Tome to Flavian set out the Catholic teaching that Christ is one Person in two natures, divine and human, and was acclaimed at the Council of Chalcedon in 451. He met Attila the Hun in 452, after which Attila withdrew from Italy, and in 455 he persuaded the Vandals to spare Rome's people from slaughter during their sack of the city.

sections.h2: From Deacon to Bishop of Rome
paras: Leo was already a respected deacon of the Roman church, consulted by figures such as John Cassian and Cyril of Alexandria, when Sixtus III died in 440. He was in Gaul on a diplomatic mission for the imperial court at the time, and the Roman clergy elected him in his absence.

His sermons and letters reveal a pastor convinced that the bishop of Rome carries on the ministry of St. Peter. He taught that Peter continues to speak and act through his successors, and he worked to apply that conviction throughout the West, including in a dispute with Bishop Hilary of Arles that ended with an imperial decree in 445 supporting Roman authority over Western bishops.

sections.h2: The Tome and the Council of Chalcedon
paras: In 448, the monk Eutyches of Constantinople taught that after the Incarnation Christ had only one nature. Archbishop Flavian condemned him, and Leo responded in 449 with a letter to Flavian known as the Tome, explaining that Christ is one divine Person in whom the divine and human natures remain whole and unconfused.

That year a council at Ephesus, dominated by Dioscorus of Alexandria, refused to read the Tome, restored Eutyches, and mistreated Flavian, who died soon after. Leo denounced it as a latrocinium, a gathering of robbers, and the name Robber Council stuck.

Under a new emperor, the Council of Chalcedon met in 451 with Leo's legates present. When the Tome was read, the bishops acclaimed it, declaring that Peter had spoken through Leo. Chalcedon's definition of Christ as one Person in two natures became the standard of Christological faith. Leo, however, refused to approve the council's twenty-eighth canon, which raised Constantinople's rank at the expense of older sees.

sections.h2: Attila at the Mincio and the Vandal Sack of 455
paras: In 452, Attila invaded northern Italy. Leo traveled with two imperial officials, the former consul Avienus and the prefect Trygetius, to meet him near the Mincio River. Attila withdrew. Ancient accounts credit Leo's intervention, while historians add that famine and disease in Attila's army probably also played a role. Later legend added the appearance of Peter and Paul, which is not part of the earliest sources.

In 455, the Vandal king Gaiseric captured Rome. Leo met him and obtained a promise that the city would not be burned and its inhabitants not massacred. The Vandals still plundered Rome for two weeks, but Leo's intervention spared much loss of life.

sections.h2: Sermons, Letters, and a Doctor of the Church
paras: Leo left a large body of sermons, many preached on the great feasts of the liturgical year, and a substantial collection of letters. His Latin is concise and rhythmic, and his Christmas and Lenten sermons are still read in the Liturgy of the Hours.

He also acted against the Manichaeans in Rome and dealt with ecclesiastical questions across Italy, Gaul, Spain, and North Africa. Leo died on November 10, 461, and was the first pope buried at St. Peter's Basilica itself. Pope Benedict XIV declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1754. His feast is November 10 in the West; Eastern Christians honor him on February 18.

keyFacts: Pope from 440 to 461; elected while on a mission in Gaul
His Tome to Flavian (449) defined Christ as one Person in two natures
His teaching was acclaimed at the Council of Chalcedon (451)
Met Attila in 452 and persuaded the Vandal king Gaiseric to spare Rome's people in 455
Declared a Doctor of the Church in 1754; feast day November 10

faqs.question: How did Pope Leo the Great stop Attila the Hun?
faqs.answer: In 452 Leo met Attila near the Mincio River with two imperial envoys, and Attila withdrew from Italy. Ancient writers credit Leo; historians note that famine and disease in Attila's army likely contributed.

faqs.question: What is the Tome of Leo?
faqs.answer: It is Leo's 449 letter to Archbishop Flavian of Constantinople explaining that Christ is one Person with a complete divine nature and a complete human nature. The Council of Chalcedon accepted it as an expression of the true faith.

faqs.question: Why is Leo I called the Great?
faqs.answer: He earned the title for his doctrinal leadership at Chalcedon, his defense of Rome against Attila and the Vandals, and his writings and pastoral governance. Only a few popes are commonly called the Great.

directAnswer: St. Hilarius was a native of Sardinia who served as pope from 461 to 468. As a deacon he had been Pope Leo I's legate to the so-called Robber Council of Ephesus in 449, where he narrowly escaped harm. As pope he continued Leo's policies, regulated church affairs in Gaul and Spain, and built oratories at the Lateran baptistery.

paras: In 449, Leo sent the deacon Hilarius as one of his representatives to a council at Ephesus called to judge Eutyches. The assembly, dominated by Dioscorus of Alexandria, overrode the Roman legates, and Hilarius protested against the condemnation of Archbishop Flavian.

Fearing for his safety, he fled and made his way back to Rome by hidden routes. As pope, he built an oratory at the Lateran baptistery dedicated to St. John the Evangelist, with an inscription thanking the apostle as his deliverer. The inscription still survives.

sections.h2: Synods and Church Order in the West
paras: Hilarius succeeded Leo in November 461 and devoted much of his short reign to church discipline in Gaul and Spain. He intervened in disputes over the see of Narbonne and over Bishop Mamertus of Vienne, who had consecrated a bishop outside his jurisdiction, and he insisted that metropolitans respect the boundaries of their provinces.

At a Roman synod in November 465, whose acts survive, he addressed irregular episcopal appointments in Spain, including bishops naming their own successors. When Emperor Anthemius showed favor to a heretical adviser, Hilarius reportedly challenged him publicly at St. Peter's. He died in February 468 and was buried at St. Lawrence Outside the Walls.

keyFacts: Pope from 461 to 468; born in Sardinia
As a deacon, served as Leo I's legate to the Robber Council of Ephesus (449)
Built Lateran oratories, including one thanking St. John the Evangelist
Held a Roman synod in 465 on church order in Spain
Feast day: February 28

faqs.question: Why did Pope Hilarius build an oratory to St. John the Evangelist?
faqs.answer: He credited St. John with his safe escape from the Robber Council of Ephesus in 449. The oratory's surviving inscription thanks John as his liberator.

faqs.question: What did Pope Hilarius do as pope?
faqs.answer: He continued Leo the Great's policies, enforced church order in Gaul and Spain, held a Roman synod in 465, and enriched the Lateran with new oratories.

directAnswer: St. Simplicius, from Tivoli near Rome, was pope from 468 to 483, the period when the last Western Roman emperor was deposed in 476 and Odoacer took control of Italy. He defended the Council of Chalcedon against Monophysite pressure in the East and dedicated the circular church of Santo Stefano Rotondo in Rome.

sections.h2: The End of the Western Empire
paras: Simplicius became pope in March 468. Eight years later, in 476, the Germanic commander Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus and ruled Italy as king, a moment often taken as the end of the Western Roman Empire.
Odoacer was an Arian Christian, but he generally left the Catholic church of Rome undisturbed. The pope increasingly became the most prominent native authority in the city.

In the Eastern churches, opponents of the Council of Chalcedon held the sees of Alexandria and Antioch at various times. Simplicius wrote repeatedly to the emperors and to Acacius, patriarch of Constantinople, urging that Chalcedon be upheld and that its opponents, such as Timothy Aelurus and Peter Mongus in Alexandria, be removed.

In 482, Emperor Zeno issued the Henotikon, a compromise document meant to satisfy both sides by avoiding Chalcedon. Simplicius was also drawn into the case of John Talaia, a Chalcedonian bishop of Alexandria who was expelled and fled to Rome. The tensions of these years led to the Acacian schism under his successor.

Simplicius dedicated Santo Stefano Rotondo on the Caelian Hill, a striking circular church, and converted a hall on the Esquiline into the church of Sant'Andrea Catabarbara. According to the Liber Pontificalis, he arranged for clergy to take turns at the great cemetery basilicas so that baptism and penance were always available. He died on March 10, 483, and was buried at St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Pope from 468 to 483; from Tivoli
Reigned when Odoacer deposed the last Western emperor in 476
Defended the Council of Chalcedon against Monophysite bishops in the East
Dedicated Santo Stefano Rotondo on the Caelian Hill
Feast day: March 10

faqs.question: Was Pope Simplicius pope when the Roman Empire fell?
faqs.answer: Yes. He was pope in 476, when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, the last Western emperor, and ruled Italy as king.

faqs.question: What church did Pope Simplicius build?
faqs.answer: He dedicated Santo Stefano Rotondo, a circular church on Rome's Caelian Hill, and also established the church of Sant'Andrea Catabarbara on the Esquiline.

directAnswer: St. Felix III was a Roman of noble family who served as pope from 483 to 492. He excommunicated Patriarch Acacius of Constantinople in 484 for supporting Emperor Zeno's Henotikon, beginning the Acacian schism between Rome and the East that lasted until 519. He was an ancestor of Pope St. Gregory the Great.

paras: Felix became pope in March 483, shortly after Emperor Zeno issued the Henotikon, a doctrinal compromise that sidestepped the Council of Chalcedon. Patriarch Acacius of Constantinople supported it and entered communion with Peter Mongus of Alexandria, whom Rome considered a heretic.

Felix sent two bishops, Vitalis and Misenus, to Constantinople to demand that Acacius explain himself. Under pressure there, they communicated with Acacius's party. On their return, a Roman synod deposed them, and in 484 Felix excommunicated Acacius. The break, known as the Acacian schism, outlasted both men and was healed only under Pope Hormisdas in 519.

sections.h2: Family, Africa, and a Confusing Number
paras: Felix was a widower with children when he became pope. Gregory the Great, writing a century later, refers to him as his ancestor, usually understood as his great-great-grandfather. The Liber Pontificalis says he came from a Roman senatorial family.

He also dealt with the aftermath of the Vandal persecution in North Africa, where some Catholics had been forcibly rebaptized by Arians; a Roman synod set terms of penance for their reconciliation. Felix is sometimes called Felix II because the earlier Felix, installed during the exile of Liberius, is now regarded as an antipope. He died on March 1, 492, and was buried at St. Paul Outside the Walls.

keyFacts: Pope from 483 to 492; from a Roman noble family
Excommunicated Patriarch Acacius in 484, beginning the Acacian schism
Set penances for Africans forcibly rebaptized during the Vandal persecution
Ancestor of Pope St. Gregory the Great
Sometimes numbered Felix II; feast day March 1

faqs.question: What was the Acacian schism?
faqs.answer: It was a break in communion between Rome and Constantinople that began when Felix III excommunicated Patriarch Acacius in 484 for backing the Henotikon. It ended in 519 under Pope Hormisdas.

faqs.question: Why is Pope Felix III sometimes called Felix II?
faqs.answer: The Felix installed during Pope Liberius's exile is now counted as an antipope. Lists that omit him number this pope as Felix II, but the official numbering keeps Felix III.

faqs.question: Was Pope Felix III related to Gregory the Great?
faqs.answer: Yes. Gregory the Great describes him as an ancestor, usually identified as his great-great-grandfather. Felix had been married with children before becoming pope.

directAnswer: St. Gelasius I was pope from 492 to 496 and one of the most important theologians among the early popes. In a letter to Emperor Anastasius I he set out the classic distinction between the sacred authority of bishops and the royal power of rulers. Ancient sources describe him as African by birth, and he was the last pope known to have been born on that continent.

sections.h2: The Two Powers: Gelasius's Letter to Anastasius
paras: In 494 Gelasius wrote to Emperor Anastasius I in Constantinople. The letter, known by its opening words Duo sunt, explained that the world is governed chiefly by two powers: the consecrated authority of bishops and the royal power of rulers.

Gelasius told the emperor that, while bishops obey imperial laws in temporal matters, rulers must submit to bishops in what concerns the sacraments and salvation, and that the responsibility of priests is weightier because they must answer to God even for kings. The letter became a foundational text for medieval thinking about the relationship between church and state.

sections.h2: Upholding Rome Against the Acacian Party
paras: Gelasius had served as a close adviser to Felix III and drafted many of his letters. As pope he maintained the excommunication of the late Acacius and refused to remove his name from the Roman condemnations, even as Anastasius pressed for compromise.

He wrote extensively on the question, insisting that the Roman see had the right to judge appeals from all churches and was itself judged by no one. Records of a Roman synod in 495 show the clergy hailing him as Vicar of Christ, one of the earliest such uses of the title for a pope.

sections.h2: Lupercalia, the Eucharist, and Care for the Poor
paras: In Rome, some Christians still took part in the Lupercalia, a pagan February festival. Gelasius wrote against a senator who defended it and worked to end Christian involvement, and the festival disappears from the record after his time.

Finding that Manichaeans in Rome refused to drink from the chalice, he ordered that Communion be received under both kinds, so as to expose and exclude their practice. He wrote theological treatises against Eutyches and Nestorius and set times for ordinations in a letter to bishops of southern Italy.

He used church resources to feed the poor during a period of shortage under Theodoric's new Ostrogothic rule. The Gelasian Sacramentary and the Decretum Gelasianum carry his name, but scholars regard both as later compilations. Gelasius died on November 21, 496.

keyFacts: Pope from 492 to 496; described as African by birth
Wrote the letter Duo sunt (494) on the two powers of bishops and rulers
Maintained the condemnation of Acacius during the Acacian schism
Opposed Christian participation in the pagan Lupercalia
Feast day: November 21

faqs.question: What is Gelasius I's doctrine of the two powers?
faqs.answer: In his 494 letter to Emperor Anastasius, Gelasius taught that the world is governed by the sacred authority of bishops and the royal power of rulers, with rulers subject to bishops in matters of faith and sacraments.

faqs.question: Did Pope Gelasius I write the Gelasian Sacramentary?
faqs.answer: No. The sacramentary is named after him, but scholars date its compilation to later centuries. The same is true of the Decretum Gelasianum, a list of accepted and rejected books.

faqs.question: Was Pope Gelasius I the last African pope?
faqs.answer: He is the last pope known to have been born in Africa. The Liber Pontificalis calls him African, though some scholars think he may have been born in Rome to African parents.

directAnswer: Anastasius II was a Roman who served as pope from 496 to 498. He tried to heal the Acacian schism with Constantinople through a more conciliatory approach, which alarmed part of the Roman clergy. After his death, divisions over that policy contributed to the double election that produced the Laurentian schism, and he is not venerated as a saint.

paras: Anastasius was elected in November 496, while relations with Constantinople were still broken over the Acacian schism. He promptly sent bishops to Emperor Anastasius I with a letter offering to restore communion if the name of the late Patriarch Acacius were removed from the Eastern church's commemorations. He also expressed willingness to accept baptisms and ordinations conferred by Acacius as valid.

In Rome, he received in communion the deacon Photinus of Thessalonica, who was associated with the Acacian side. A portion of the Roman clergy considered this a betrayal of his predecessors' firm stance and broke communion with him.

sections.h2: Death, Schism, and a Harsh Reputation
paras: Anastasius died in November 498 before any settlement was reached. The divisions his policy had exposed led to two rival elections, Symmachus and Laurentius, opening the Laurentian schism.

The Liber Pontificalis, written by authors hostile to his policy, treats him severely, and medieval writers inherited that view. Dante placed a Pope Anastasius in the Inferno, likely confusing him with the emperor of the same name. A letter congratulating the Frankish king Clovis on his baptism is sometimes attributed to him, but its authenticity is doubted. Anastasius II is not venerated as a saint in either the Latin or Eastern churches.

keyFacts: Pope from 496 to 498; Roman by birth
Sought to end the Acacian schism through negotiation
Received the deacon Photinus of Thessalonica into communion, angering some clergy
His death was followed by the Laurentian schism
Not venerated as a saint in the Latin or Eastern churches

faqs.question: Why is Pope Anastasius II not a saint?
faqs.answer: He was never venerated as one. His conciliatory approach to the Acacian schism provoked opposition in Rome, and early sources such as the Liber Pontificalis portrayed him negatively.

faqs.question: Why did Dante put Pope Anastasius in Hell?
faqs.answer: In the Inferno, Dante places a Pope Anastasius among heretics. Scholars think this rests on medieval confusion between Pope Anastasius II and Emperor Anastasius I.

directAnswer: St. Symmachus was a Sardinian-born deacon who served as pope from 498 to 514. Elected on the same day as a rival candidate, Laurentius, he spent much of his reign fighting the resulting Laurentian schism, which King Theodoric the Ostrogoth was drawn in to settle. He is also remembered for aiding exiled African bishops and for his building work at St. Peter's.

paras: When Anastasius II died in November 498, the Roman church was split over his conciliatory approach to Constantinople. On November 22, the deacon Symmachus was elected at the Lateran by the majority of clergy, while a faction favoring reconciliation with the East, supported by the senator Festus, chose the archpriest Laurentius at Santa Maria Maggiore.

Both sides appealed to Theodoric, the Arian Ostrogothic king who ruled Italy from Ravenna. Theodoric decided that the candidate consecrated first and supported by the larger party should hold the see, which favored Symmachus. In 499 a Roman synod under Symmachus issued rules against campaigning for the papacy while a pope was still living.

In 501 the Laurentian party brought charges against Symmachus, including celebrating Easter on the wrong date, misuse of church property, and moral misconduct. Theodoric summoned him to Ravenna, and Symmachus, alarmed by the proceedings, withdrew to St. Peter's. A visitor appointed by the king, Bishop Peter of Altinum, took over administration of the Roman church, and Laurentius returned to the city.

A synod of Italian bishops met in Rome. It declined to sit in judgment over the pope, declaring that the case should be left to God, and restored Symmachus to his full authority. Around this time, partisans of Symmachus circulated texts, now called the Symmachian forgeries, purporting to show that earlier popes could not be judged by anyone, an idea expressed in the principle that the first see is judged by no one.

sections.h2: The End of the Laurentian Schism
paras: For several years, Laurentius's supporters held many churches in Rome, and street violence broke out between the factions. A pro-Laurentian account, the Laurentian Fragment, survives and presents their side. Around 506 Theodoric ordered the churches returned to Symmachus, and Laurentius withdrew, ending the schism.
With the Eastern church, Symmachus maintained the firm line against the Acacian party, and relations with Emperor Anastasius I remained hostile.

When the Vandal king Thrasamund exiled Catholic bishops from North Africa to Sardinia, Symmachus sent them money and clothing. He ransomed captives taken in northern Italy and supported the poor of Rome.

He undertook building projects at St. Peter's, including facilities for pilgrims and the poor, and rebuilt or adorned several churches. In 513 he granted the pallium to Caesarius of Arles and named him his representative in Gaul, a sign of growing ties between Rome and the Gallic church. Symmachus died on July 19, 514, and was buried at St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Pope from 498 to 514; born in Sardinia
Elected the same day as rival Laurentius, beginning the Laurentian schism
King Theodoric ruled in his favor in 499 and ended the schism around 506
Supported Catholic bishops exiled from Africa by the Vandals
Granted the pallium to Caesarius of Arles; feast day July 19

faqs.question: What was the Laurentian schism?
faqs.answer: It was a split in the Roman church after rival elections of Symmachus and Laurentius in 498. Despite Theodoric's ruling for Symmachus, the conflict continued until about 506.

faqs.question: What are the Symmachian forgeries?
faqs.answer: They are documents produced by supporters of Symmachus around 501 that claimed earlier popes could not be judged by any earthly tribunal. They influenced later canon law even though they were not authentic.

faqs.question: Why did King Theodoric get involved in a papal election?
faqs.answer: Theodoric ruled Italy, and both factions appealed to him to restore order. Though an Arian, he decided between the rivals according to which candidate was consecrated first and had the larger following.

directAnswer: St. Hormisdas was pope from 514 to 523 and the pontiff who ended the 35-year Acacian schism between Rome and Constantinople. In 519 the patriarch of Constantinople signed the Formula of Hormisdas, a profession of faith affirming the Council of Chalcedon and the steadfast faith of the Roman see. Before ordination he had been married, and his son Silverius later became pope.

paras: Hormisdas came from Frosinone in Campania. Before entering the clergy he had married and fathered a son, Silverius, who would become pope in 536. As a deacon he was a trusted associate of Symmachus and had a hand in managing the church during the Laurentian troubles.
Elected on the day after Symmachus's death in July 514, he took office with Rome's internal divisions largely calmed. He worked to reconcile the remaining supporters of Laurentius.

The emperor Anastasius I, facing a revolt in the Balkans led partly in the name of Chalcedonian orthodoxy, opened negotiations with Rome. Hormisdas sent legations to Constantinople in 515 and 517, both including Bishop Ennodius of Pavia.

Hormisdas insisted on the condemnation of Acacius and acceptance of Chalcedon and the Tome of Leo. Anastasius would not agree, and the second embassy ended with the legates expelled and their documents distributed under hostile conditions. The breach remained unhealed until the emperor's death in 518.

sections.h2: The Formula of Hormisdas and the End of the Acacian Schism
paras: Anastasius's successor, Justin I, and his nephew Justinian were committed Chalcedonians. In 519, papal legates arrived in Constantinople, and on Holy Thursday, March 28, Patriarch John II signed the Formula of Hormisdas. It accepted Chalcedon, condemned Acacius and others, and declared that the Catholic faith had always been kept undefiled in the Apostolic See.

Some 2,500 Eastern bishops are said to have later subscribed, though that figure comes from later accounts. The Formula's statement on the Roman see's faithfulness was cited at the First Vatican Council in 1870 in its teaching on papal primacy and infallibility.

sections.h2: The Scythian Monks and Later Years
paras: Around the same time, a group of monks from Scythia promoted the formula that one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh, meant to defend Chalcedon against misreadings. Hormisdas was cautious and did not endorse it; it was later accepted under John II.
The Liber Pontificalis records gifts sent to St. Peter's by the Frankish king Clovis and by Emperor Justin. Hormisdas died on August 6, 523, and was buried at St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Pope from 514 to 523; from Frosinone in Campania
Married before ordination; father of Pope St. Silverius
Ended the Acacian schism in 519 with the Formula of Hormisdas
The Formula was cited at the First Vatican Council (1870)
Feast day: August 6

faqs.question: What is the Formula of Hormisdas?
faqs.answer: It is a profession of faith signed by Patriarch John II of Constantinople in 519. It accepted the Council of Chalcedon, condemned Acacius, and affirmed that the Catholic faith had always been preserved in the Apostolic See.

faqs.question: Was Pope Hormisdas married?
faqs.answer: Yes. He was married before becoming a cleric, and his son Silverius became pope in 536. This was not unusual for clergy of that era.

faqs.question: How long did the Acacian schism last?
faqs.answer: It lasted from Felix III's excommunication of Acacius in 484 until the signing of the Formula of Hormisdas in 519, about 35 years.

directAnswer: St. John I was pope from 523 to 526 and the first pope known to have traveled to Constantinople. King Theodoric sent him there to ask Emperor Justin I to ease measures against Arians, and on his return Theodoric, suspecting him of conspiring with the emperor, had him detained at Ravenna, where he died. The Church honors him as a martyr on May 18.

paras: John, born in Tuscany, was an elderly deacon when elected in August 523. Italy was ruled by Theodoric the Ostrogoth, an Arian who had long tolerated the Catholic majority. By the 520s, however, relations between Theodoric and the Roman senatorial class were deteriorating.

Theodoric suspected that leading Romans favored the Eastern emperor. He imprisoned and executed the senator and philosopher Boethius, author of The Consolation of Philosophy, and later Boethius's father-in-law Symmachus.

Emperor Justin I had begun to act against Arians in the East, closing their churches. Theodoric, himself an Arian, demanded that the pope go to Constantinople to seek relief for his coreligionists. John, accompanied by several bishops and senators, left in late 525.

In Constantinople he was received with great honor. He celebrated Easter in the city's principal church, and the Liber Pontificalis says the emperor was crowned by him, a detail historians treat cautiously. Justin agreed to return churches to the Arians but would not allow those who had converted to Catholicism to return to Arianism, which had been one of Theodoric's demands.

When John returned in 526, Theodoric regarded the warm reception in Constantinople and the partial results with suspicion. He detained the pope at Ravenna, where John died on May 18, 526, worn down by confinement and ill treatment.

His body was brought to Rome and buried in St. Peter's, and he was soon venerated as a martyr. Theodoric himself died a few months later. During John's reign, the monk Dionysius Exiguus completed his Easter tables, which counted years from the Incarnation and gave rise to the Anno Domini dating system.

keyFacts: Pope from 523 to 526; born in Tuscany
First pope known to have visited Constantinople (525–526)
Sent by King Theodoric to seek relief for Arians from Emperor Justin I
Died in detention at Ravenna in May 526; venerated as a martyr
Buried at St. Peter's; feast day May 18

faqs.question: Why did Theodoric imprison Pope John I?
faqs.answer: Theodoric suspected that John had grown too close to Emperor Justin I during his embassy to Constantinople and had not obtained everything the king demanded. He detained the pope in Ravenna, where John died.

faqs.question: Was Pope John I a martyr?
faqs.answer: He is venerated as a martyr because he died from harsh treatment while held by Theodoric. He was not executed, but his death was seen as a consequence of his fidelity.

faqs.question: What did Pope John I achieve in Constantinople?
faqs.answer: He was honored by Emperor Justin I and celebrated Easter there. Justin agreed to restore churches to Arians but refused to let converts return to Arianism.

directAnswer: St. Felix IV, from Samnium in southern Italy, was pope from 526 to 530. He was chosen with the backing of King Theodoric after John I's death, built the Basilica of Santi Cosma e Damiano in the Roman Forum, and supported Caesarius of Arles in the debates over grace that led to the Council of Orange in 529. Near death he named Boniface as his successor, a step that provoked a disputed election.

sections.h2: Santi Cosma e Damiano in the Forum
paras: Felix's most lasting monument is the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, which he established in buildings of the old Roman Forum, given for the purpose by the Ostrogothic court. Its sixth-century apse mosaic, showing Christ amid the apostles and saints, includes a figure of Felix offering a model of the church, though that portion was later restored.
It was among the first churches in the Forum, marking the Christian transformation of the ancient civic center.

sections.h2: Grace, Orange, and a Contested Succession
paras: In Gaul, Caesarius of Arles was opposing views on grace now usually called Semi-Pelagian. Felix sent him a set of propositions drawn largely from Augustine, which formed the basis of the canons adopted at the Second Council of Orange in 529. His successor confirmed that council.

Felix also obtained from the Ostrogothic regency a decree recognizing church jurisdiction over clergy. In 530, gravely ill, he named the archdeacon Boniface as his successor and gave him his pallium. Many Roman clergy objected and elected Dioscorus instead, producing a brief schism. Felix died in September 530. Beyond these episodes, little about his life is recorded.

keyFacts: Pope from 526 to 530; from Samnium
Chosen with the support of King Theodoric
Built Santi Cosma e Damiano in the Roman Forum
His propositions on grace shaped the Second Council of Orange (529)
Sometimes numbered Felix III

faqs.question: What church did Pope Felix IV build?
faqs.answer: He established Santi Cosma e Damiano in the Roman Forum, one of the first churches there. Its apse mosaic includes a restored figure of Felix presenting the church.

faqs.question: Why is Pope Felix IV sometimes called Felix III?
faqs.answer: Because the Felix installed during the exile of Pope Liberius is now considered an antipope, some lists number later popes named Felix one lower.

directAnswer: Boniface II was pope from 530 to 532 and the first pope of Germanic descent; he was born in Rome to a father with a Gothic name. Designated by Felix IV, he faced the rival candidate Dioscorus until Dioscorus died weeks later. Boniface confirmed the canons of the Second Council of Orange on grace.

paras: Felix IV, near death, named the archdeacon Boniface as his successor. The majority of the Roman clergy, rejecting this unprecedented designation, elected the deacon Dioscorus. Both were consecrated on September 22, 530.

Dioscorus died on October 14, leaving Boniface unopposed. Boniface required the clergy who had supported his rival to sign a condemnation of Dioscorus's memory. Later he tried to name the deacon Vigilius as his own successor at a Roman synod, but opposition forced him to withdraw and burn the decree.

sections.h2: Orange and the Anno Domini Question
paras: In 531, Boniface wrote to Caesarius of Arles approving the canons of the Second Council of Orange, which taught that the beginning of faith is itself a gift of grace. The Liber Pontificalis also says he helped relieve the clergy during a famine.
