Some popular lists credit Boniface with changing the way years were numbered. The Anno Domini count came from the Easter tables of Dionysius Exiguus in 525, before Boniface was pope; his own role in its adoption is not established. Boniface died in October 532. He is not venerated as a saint.

keyFacts: Pope from 530 to 532; first pope of Germanic descent
Designated by Felix IV; contested by Dioscorus until Dioscorus died
Attempted, then withdrew, the designation of Vigilius as successor
Confirmed the Second Council of Orange's teaching on grace in 531
Not venerated as a saint

faqs.question: Why is Boniface II called the first Germanic pope?
faqs.answer: He was born in Rome, but his father bore a Gothic name, which is why he is considered the first pope of Germanic ancestry.

faqs.question: Did Pope Boniface II introduce Anno Domini dating?
faqs.answer: No clear evidence supports that. The Anno Domini system came from Dionysius Exiguus's Easter tables, written in 525, before Boniface became pope.

directAnswer: John II was pope from 533 to 535 and the first pope to take a new name upon election. Born Mercurius, a Roman priest of San Clemente, he chose the name John because his birth name recalled the pagan god Mercury. His brief reign saw a royal decree against simony in papal elections and his approval of a key Christological formula sent by Emperor Justinian.

paras: Mercurius was a priest of the Roman church of San Clemente, where inscriptions bearing his name have been found. After Boniface II's death, the papal see stood vacant for about two and a half months amid reports of bribery. When Mercurius was finally chosen in January 533, he took the name John, judging a pagan god's name unsuitable for the bishop of Rome.
The vacancy prompted the Ostrogothic king Athalaric to issue a decree against buying and selling votes in papal elections, confirming an earlier Roman senate resolution.

Emperor Justinian sent John a profession of faith including the formula that one of the Holy Trinity suffered in the flesh, which Pope Hormisdas had declined to endorse. In 534 John accepted it as orthodox and rejected the monks in Constantinople who opposed it. Justinian included his correspondence with John in his law code.

John also dealt with Bishop Contumeliosus of Riez in Gaul, accused of serious misconduct, supporting Caesarius of Arles in removing him from his duties. John died in May 535 and was buried at St. Peter's. He is not listed among the saints, and little more is known of him.

keyFacts: Pope from 533 to 535; born Mercurius
First pope to adopt a new name on election
Former priest of the Roman church of San Clemente
King Athalaric issued a decree against simony in papal elections after his election
Approved Justinian's profession of faith in 534

faqs.question: Why did Pope John II change his name?
faqs.answer: His birth name, Mercurius, came from the Roman god Mercury. He chose John instead, making him the first pope to take a new name on election.

faqs.question: What is Pope John II's connection to San Clemente?
faqs.answer: Before his election, he was a priest of San Clemente in Rome, and inscriptions there record his name as Mercurius.

directAnswer: St. Agapetus I was pope for less than a year, from 535 to 536. He traveled to Constantinople at the request of the Ostrogothic king Theodahad to try to prevent Justinian's invasion of Italy; that mission failed, but while there he deposed Patriarch Anthimus for heresy and personally consecrated his successor Menas. He died in Constantinople in April 536.

sections.h2: A Roman Archdeacon and a Library Plan
paras: Agapetus was the son of a Roman priest named Gordianus and had served as archdeacon. One of his first acts was to burn publicly the document in which Boniface II had compelled the clergy to condemn Dioscorus, a gesture of reconciliation.

With the statesman Cassiodorus, he planned a Christian school of higher learning in Rome. The project was overtaken by war, but Agapetus did establish a library at his family property on the Caelian Hill, and an inscription associated with it survives.

sections.h2: Mission to Justinian and the Deposition of Anthimus
paras: In 535, Justinian's general Belisarius was preparing to retake Italy from the Goths. King Theodahad sent Agapetus to Constantinople to negotiate peace, and the pope reportedly had to pledge church property to pay for the journey. Justinian would not call off the campaign.

In Constantinople, Agapetus found that Patriarch Anthimus had been transferred from another see and was suspected of rejecting Chalcedon. He refused communion with Anthimus, who was removed, and in March 536 consecrated Menas as patriarch. He died in Constantinople on April 22, 536; his body was returned to Rome and buried at St. Peter's. He is honored on April 22 and September 20 in the West and on April 17 in the East.

keyFacts: Pope from 535 to 536; son of the Roman priest Gordianus
Planned a Christian school with Cassiodorus and founded a library on the Caelian
Traveled to Constantinople in 536 on behalf of King Theodahad
Deposed Patriarch Anthimus and consecrated Menas
Died in Constantinople; buried at St. Peter's

faqs.question: Why did Pope Agapetus I go to Constantinople?
faqs.answer: The Ostrogothic king Theodahad sent him to persuade Emperor Justinian not to invade Italy. Justinian refused, but Agapetus used the visit to act against Patriarch Anthimus.

faqs.question: Who was Anthimus, deposed by Agapetus?
faqs.answer: Anthimus was patriarch of Constantinople and was suspected of rejecting the Council of Chalcedon. Agapetus refused communion with him, he was removed, and Agapetus consecrated Menas in his place.

directAnswer: St. Silverius, son of Pope Hormisdas, was pope from 536 until he was deposed in March 537. Caught between the Goths and the Byzantine general Belisarius, he was accused of treason, removed from office, and sent into exile, where he died. He is venerated as a martyr, with a feast day of June 20.

paras: Silverius was a subdeacon when the Ostrogothic king Theodahad pressed for his election in June 536 after Agapetus died in Constantinople. His father, Hormisdas, had been pope before him, having married before ordination.

Within months, the Byzantine general Belisarius entered Rome in December 536, and the city was soon besieged by the new Gothic king, Witiges. Silverius found himself in a city occupied by imperial forces while the empress Theodora pursued her own aims for the papacy.

Theodora wanted the deposed Patriarch Anthimus restored and favored the deacon Vigilius, who was then in Constantinople, as a more pliable pope. In March 537 Silverius was accused of corresponding with the Goths to betray the city; the Liber Pontificalis says the letters were forged. Belisarius stripped him of his office and sent him to Patara in Lycia.

The local bishop protested to Justinian, who ordered an inquiry and sent Silverius back to Italy. Vigilius, now installed as pope, had him taken to the island of Palmarola in the Pontine group, where he died later in 537, by tradition from starvation. He is honored as a martyr and as patron of the island of Ponza.

keyFacts: Pope from June 536 until deposed around March 537
Son of Pope St. Hormisdas
Accused of treason and deposed by the general Belisarius
Died in exile on the island of Palmarola in 537
Venerated as a martyr; feast day June 20

faqs.question: Why was Pope Silverius deposed?
faqs.answer: He was accused of plotting to hand Rome to the besieging Goths. Ancient sources say the letters used as evidence were forged, and the empress Theodora wanted Vigilius in his place.

faqs.question: Was Pope Silverius the son of a pope?
faqs.answer: Yes. His father was Pope St. Hormisdas, who had married before entering the clergy. Silverius was born before his father's ordination.

directAnswer: Vigilius was pope from 537 to 555, one of the most troubled pontificates of late antiquity. Installed after the deposition of Silverius under Byzantine pressure, he spent years in Constantinople during the Three Chapters controversy, reversing his position more than once before accepting the decisions of the Second Council of Constantinople in 553. He died at Syracuse on his way home and is not venerated as a saint.

paras: Vigilius came from a Roman aristocratic family. As a deacon he was briefly named successor by Boniface II, who withdrew the designation, and he later served as papal representative in Constantinople, where he gained the confidence of Empress Theodora.

Writers of the time, including Liberatus and Procopius, report that Theodora backed him in return for a promise to support the deposed Patriarch Anthimus; historians weigh these accounts carefully, as some were hostile. After Belisarius deposed Silverius in March 537, Vigilius was installed as bishop of Rome. Silverius's death later that year removed any rival claim, and Vigilius was recognized by the Roman clergy.

To win over opponents of Chalcedon, Justinian issued an edict around 544 condemning three sets of writings associated with Antiochene theology: the person and works of Theodore of Mopsuestia, certain writings of Theodoret of Cyrus, and a letter of Ibas of Edessa. Western bishops objected that this undermined Chalcedon, which had received Theodoret and Ibas.

In 545 Vigilius was taken from Rome and, after a stay in Sicily, arrived in Constantinople in 547. In 548 he issued a document called the Iudicatum condemning the Three Chapters while affirming Chalcedon. The reaction in the West was severe; a council in Africa broke communion with him, and he withdrew the document.

sections.h2: Conflict with Justinian and the Council of 553
paras: When Justinian published a further condemnation in 551 without waiting for a council, Vigilius protested and took refuge in a church in Constantinople and later in the Church of St. Euphemia at Chalcedon. Accounts say imperial soldiers tried to drag him from the altar.

Justinian convened the Second Council of Constantinople in 553. Vigilius refused to attend and issued a Constitutum that rejected the writings in question but declined to condemn the persons of Theodoret and Ibas. The council condemned the Three Chapters and removed his name from the diptychs. Isolated and in poor health, he accepted the council's decisions in documents issued in December 553 and February 554.

With Justinian's permission to return, Vigilius obtained from the emperor the Pragmatic Sanction of 554, which regulated the government of reconquered Italy. He set out for Rome but died at Syracuse in Sicily on June 7, 555. His body was brought to Rome and buried in the church of San Marcello on the Via Salaria.

His acceptance of the council was rejected for decades by churches in northern Italy, leading to a lasting schism centered on Aquileia. Vigilius's career is often studied as an example of the pressures placed on the papacy by Byzantine emperors.

keyFacts: Pope from 537 to 555, installed after the deposition of Silverius
Spent roughly eight years in Constantinople during the Three Chapters controversy
Issued the Iudicatum (548), later withdrew it, then accepted the 553 council
Pope during the Second Council of Constantinople (553)
Died at Syracuse in 555; not venerated as a saint

faqs.question: What was the Three Chapters controversy?
faqs.answer: It was a dispute over Justinian's condemnation of writings by Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret of Cyrus, and Ibas of Edessa. Many Western bishops feared this weakened the Council of Chalcedon.

faqs.question: Did Pope Vigilius attend the Second Council of Constantinople?
faqs.answer: No. He was in Constantinople but refused to attend. He later accepted the council's condemnation of the Three Chapters in 553 and 554.

faqs.question: Why did Pope Vigilius change his position so often?
faqs.answer: He was caught between Justinian's pressure in Constantinople and strong Western opposition to condemning the Three Chapters. He tried to protect Chalcedon's authority while dealing with an emperor who controlled his movements.

directAnswer: Pelagius I was pope from 556 to 561. A Roman deacon who had represented the papacy in Constantinople, he first opposed and then accepted the condemnation of the Three Chapters, and Emperor Justinian chose him to succeed Vigilius. As pope he faced distrust in the West, worked to restore the finances of the Roman church after the Gothic War, and began the church of Santi Apostoli.

sections.h2: Deacon, Diplomat, and Defender of Rome
paras: Pelagius, from a Roman family, served as papal representative in Constantinople and influenced Justinian's condemnation of Origenist teachings in 543. During the Gothic siege of Rome in 546, he used his own wealth to feed the starving population and negotiated with the Gothic king Totila, who sent him to Constantinople on a peace mission.

He initially sided with Western opposition to condemning the Three Chapters and wrote a defense of them. After the Second Council of Constantinople, he changed his position, and Justinian, recognizing his ability, chose him to succeed Vigilius.

Pelagius returned to Rome in 556, where many clergy and laypeople blamed him for Vigilius's hardships and doubted his orthodoxy. Few bishops would consecrate him; the Liber Pontificalis says only two bishops and a priest from Ostia took part. He made a public oath at St. Peter's that he had done no harm to Vigilius, and declared his loyalty to the four ecumenical councils.

Bishops in northern Italy and parts of Gaul remained distrustful, and the sees of Milan and Aquileia broke communion over the Three Chapters. Pelagius reorganized the papal estates, restored church administration, and aided the poor after years of war. He began the church of Santi Apostoli in Rome, completed by his successor. Pelagius died in March 561 and was buried at St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Pope from 556 to 561
Former papal representative in Constantinople
Fed starving Romans during Totila's siege in 546
Chosen by Emperor Justinian after accepting the condemnation of the Three Chapters
Began the church of Santi Apostoli in Rome

faqs.question: Why was Pope Pelagius I distrusted when he became pope?
faqs.answer: He had shifted his position on the Three Chapters and was suspected of involvement in Vigilius's mistreatment. To answer those doubts, he swore a public oath at St. Peter's and affirmed his loyalty to the four ecumenical councils.

faqs.question: Did Pope Pelagius I build Santi Apostoli?
faqs.answer: He began the church of Santi Apostoli in Rome, and it was completed under his successor, John III.
